To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the incidence of overeducation and overskilling is higher than the incidence of mismatch with respect to either skill or education only; 2) the incidence of overskilling is negatively correlated with the incidence of overducation; 3) the incidence of mismatch is higher in countries with higher levels of education, lower unemployment rates, lower GDP per capita and higher levels of inequality; and 4) the incidence of both overeducation and overskill increases with age, and decreases with years
occupational mismatch is a complex phenomenon, and that it can be measured with different approaches, depending on the policy goal.
the conceptualisation of occupational mismatch matters and that education and skills mismatch do not measure exactly the same phenomenon.
In summary, our research is concerned with
two important questions: How can occupational mismatch be conceptualised and measured? And, how can we explain the differences in the prevalence of occupational mismatch across Europe?

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
occupational mismatch is not only a problem of the labour market but also of the educational systems.
the measurement of occupational mismatch is not a trivial exercise and that the choice of the conceptualisation and the measurement approach can significantly influence the outcomes.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the conceptualisation of occupational mismatch is crucial and the use of a single indicator is not recommended.
the measurement of occupational mismatch is not a trivial task and that the choice of the indicator to be used is of utmost importance.
the measurement of occupational mismatch is a crucial first step towards understanding its causes and consequences and developing policies that aim at reducing this labour market inefficacy.
